How to Calculate Your Hourly Rate From Annual Salary

Quick Answer

Divide your annual gross salary by your total scheduled hours for the year — $60,000 ÷ 2,080 hours is $28.85 an hour.

You know your annual salary, but what does it actually pay per hour? To calculate your hourly rate from your salary, divide your annual gross salary by the hours you work in a year. On a standard full-time schedule of 40 hours a week across 52 weeks, that means dividing by 2,080 hours — so a $60,000 salary works out to about $28.85 an hour.

But 2,080 hours is only a starting point. Your real hourly rate changes a lot if your job expects 45 or 50 hours a week, if you take unpaid leave, or if your pay includes bonuses and paid time off. This guide walks through the formula, the schedule adjustments, real salary comparisons, and the mistakes people usually make, so you can figure out what your time is actually worth.

Quick Answer

How Do You Calculate Hourly Rate From Salary?

To calculate your hourly rate from your salary, divide your annual gross salary by the total hours you're scheduled to work in a year.

The Standard Calculation Formula Hourly Rate = Annual Gross Salary ÷ Annual Work Hours
For the standard full-time schedule (40 hours/week × 52 weeks = 2,080 hours): Hourly Rate = Annual Salary ÷ 2,080
For example, at a salary of $60,000 per year: $60,000 ÷ 2,080 hours = $28.85 / hour

Note: This is your gross hourly rate, before federal, state, and local income taxes, FICA, and other deductions come out.

The Salary-to-Hourly Formula

The math is just division. The part that matters is getting the two numbers right: what you're paid, and how many hours you actually work for it.

Universal Mathematical Blueprint Applicable to all pay structures
ANNUAL SALARY

ANNUAL WORK HOURS
= HOURLY RATE

For a standard full-time job — 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year:

Annual Salary ÷ (40 Hours/Week × 52 Weeks/Year) = Hourly Rate
Annual Salary ÷ 2,080 Hours = Hourly Rate

Here's what each part means:

  • Annual Gross Salary (Numerator): Your full salary for the year, before taxes or any deductions come out.
  • Annual Work Hours (Denominator): The hours you're scheduled to work in that same year. The usual full-time standard is 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks).

Want to try your own numbers? Use the Hourly Wage Converter or go straight to the Salary to Hourly Calculator.

Why 2,080 Hours Is Used to Calculate an Hourly Rate

If you've ever read a job offer or a pay stub, you've probably seen the number 2,080. So where does it come from, and why does payroll use it everywhere?

The math is simple:

Standard Payroll Baseline The 2,080-Hour Derivation
40 Hours Per Week × 52 Weeks Per Year = 2,080 Scheduled Hours

That's five 8-hour days a week, all 52 weeks of the year (8 × 5 × 52 = 2,080).

But keep in mind: 2,080 is a payroll baseline, not a rule about how much anyone actually works. Payroll teams use it to keep pay packages consistent, but real schedules vary a lot:

  • Unpaid Leave: Take 2 weeks unpaid and you work 50 paid weeks (2,000 hours). On a fixed $60,000 salary, your rate while you're actually working is $60,000 ÷ 2,000 = $30.00/hour.
  • 35-Hour Workweeks: Plenty of companies treat 35 hours a week as full-time. Over 52 weeks that's 1,820 hours a year, so a $60,000 salary works out to $60,000 ÷ 1,820 = $32.97/hour.
  • Overtime Schedules: If an exempt salaried job expects 45 hours every week, that's 2,340 hours a year, and the same $60,000 salary drops to $60,000 ÷ 2,340 = $25.64/hour.

How to Calculate Hourly Rate Step by Step

Here's how to work out your real hourly rate from any salary, in five steps:

1

Step 1: Identify Your Annual Gross Salary

Start with your total base salary for the year, before deductions. Leave bonuses out unless you want your total compensation rate. Example: $60,000.

2

Step 2: Determine Your Average Weekly Working Hours

Count the hours you actually work in a typical week. Full-time is usually 40 hours, but use your real schedule if it's 35, 45, or 50. Example: 40 hours per week.

3

Step 3: Determine Your Paid Weeks Per Year

Count your paid weeks for the year. Paid time off counts, so that's usually all 52 weeks. Only subtract weeks you take unpaid. Example: 52 paid weeks.

4

Step 4: Calculate Your Annual Scheduled Hours

Multiply weekly hours by paid weeks: Weekly Hours × Paid Weeks = Annual Hours. Example: 40 × 52 = 2,080 annual hours.

5

Step 5: Divide Annual Salary by Annual Scheduled Hours

Divide your annual gross salary by your total annual hours: $60,000 ÷ 2,080 = $28.846. Round to two decimals: $28.85 per hour.

How Different Work Schedules Change Your Hourly Rate

Here's the thing most people miss: a salary on its own doesn't tell you what you're really earning per hour. Two people on the same $60,000 salary can have very different hourly rates, depending on how many hours their jobs actually demand.

See what happens to a fixed $60,000 salary as the weekly hours change:

Weekly Work Schedule Annual Hours (52 Weeks) Effective Hourly Rate Difference vs 40-Hr Benchmark
20 hrs / week (Part-Time) 1,040 hrs $57.69 / hr +$28.84 / hr (+100%)
30 hrs / week 1,560 hrs $38.46 / hr +$9.61 / hr (+33.3%)
35 hrs / week (Standard Full-Time in some sectors) 1,820 hrs $32.97 / hr +$4.12 / hr (+14.3%)
40 hrs / week (Standard Baseline) 2,080 hrs $28.85 / hr Baseline benchmark
45 hrs / week (Overtime/Extended) 2,340 hrs $25.64 / hr -$3.21 / hr (-11.1%)
50 hrs / week (High-Demand Salaried) 2,600 hrs $23.08 / hr -$5.77 / hr (-20.0%)

Look at the difference: an exempt employee on $60,000 who regularly works 50 hours a week instead of 40 sees their real rate fall from $28.85 down to $23.08. That's 520 extra hours a year with no extra pay — about three full months of work, unpaid.

How Unpaid Time Off Changes Your Effective Rate

Unpaid time off plays out differently depending on whether you're paid hourly or on a fixed salary:

Scenario A: 52 Paid Weeks

Standard Full-Time Year

Weeks Worked: 52 weeks
Annual Hours: 2,080 hours
Annual Salary: $60,000.00
Effective Hourly Rate: $28.85 / hour
Scenario B: 50 Paid Weeks

Two Weeks Unpaid Leave

Weeks Worked: 50 weeks
Annual Hours: 2,000 hours
Annual Salary: $60,000.00
Effective Hourly Rate: $30.00 / hour

If your $60,000 salary covers only 50 weeks of work — common for academic or seasonal salaried roles — your hourly earnings while working rise from $28.85 to $30.00 an hour. For an hourly worker it's the opposite: two unpaid weeks off cuts annual earnings from $52,000 to $50,000, as explained in our guide on how to convert hourly pay to annual salary.

How PTO and Paid Vacation Affect the Calculation

One question comes up all the time: should you subtract paid vacation or PTO when you work out your hourly rate?

Essential Payroll Rule Paid Leave vs. Unpaid Leave

Never subtract paid vacation or PTO from the standard 2,080-hour baseline. Paid time off is already part of your annual salary — when you take a paid vacation day, your paycheck stays the same.

Here's how the two kinds of leave compare:

  • Paid Vacation / PTO: You take 3 weeks off and still get all 26 biweekly paychecks for the year. Your salary stays $60,000, and your standard hourly rate stays $28.85 on 2,080 paid hours.
  • Unpaid Time Off: You take 3 weeks unpaid, your employer holds back pay for those weeks, and you only get paid for 49 weeks. Your gross pay drops with it.

How Overtime Changes the Real Value of a Salary

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), federal law sorts employees into two groups for overtime:

  • Exempt Salaried Employees: Most executive, administrative, professional, and outside sales employees who meet the salary and job-duties tests are exempt from overtime. Whether they work 40, 50, or 60 hours in a week, they get the same fixed salary, no extra pay. So every extra hour cuts their real hourly rate.
  • Non-Exempt Salaried Employees: Employees who don't meet the FLSA exemption rules must get 1.5 times their regular hourly rate for every hour past 40 in a workweek.

Which group you're in decides which rule applies. If you're not sure where your job falls, read our guide to exempt vs. non-exempt status and the overtime rights that come with it before you do the math below.

Say you're a non-exempt employee on a $60,000 base salary ($28.85 an hour regular rate) and you work 5 overtime hours a week:

Overtime Pay Formula Time-and-a-Half Rate
Overtime Rate = $28.85 × 1.5 = $43.28 / overtime hour
5 Extra Hours / Week = $216.40 / week
Annual Overtime Earnings = $216.40 × 52 Weeks = $11,252.80
Total Gross Annual Compensation = $60,000 + $11,252.80 = $71,252.80

To try your own overtime numbers, with time-and-a-half or double-time, use our free Overtime Calculator.

Gross Hourly Rate vs. Take-Home Hourly Rate

When you work out that a $60,000 salary is $28.85 an hour, remember: that's your gross hourly equivalent. It's not what actually lands in your bank account on payday.

Before payday, a few things come out of that gross pay:

  • Federal Income Tax: Taxed in progressive brackets from 10% to 37%, depending on your filing status and taxable income.
  • State and Local Income Taxes: From 0% in states with no income tax (like Texas, Florida, and Washington) to over 10% in states like California and New York.
  • FICA Taxes: Federal payroll taxes: 6.2% for Social Security (up to the annual wage cap) and 1.45% for Medicare.
  • Pre-Tax Deductions: Health, dental, and vision insurance premiums, Health Savings Accounts (HSA), Flexible Spending Accounts (FSA), and traditional 401(k) or 403(b) retirement contributions.
  • Post-Tax Deductions: Roth 401(k) contributions, union dues, disability insurance, or wage garnishments.
Take-Home Reality Gross vs. Net Breakdown

On a $60,000 salary ($28.85 gross an hour), someone with average federal and state taxes and modest health costs usually takes home about $21.50 to $23.20 per hour net. To run your own gross pay with your deductions, try our Paycheck Calculator (gross-pay estimates only; it does not calculate tax withholdings).

Salary vs. Hourly Pay: Real-World Offer Comparison

This is where knowing your hourly rate really pays off. A bigger headline salary doesn't always mean more pay for your time. We run the numbers on both models in our worked comparison of a $32 hourly rate versus a $65,000 salary, after taxes as well as before.

Offer A: Higher Headline Salary

Corporate Salaried Position

Stated Annual Salary: $60,000.00 / year
Expected Weekly Hours: 40 hours / week
Paid Weeks: 52 weeks (with PTO)
Annual Working Hours: 2,080 hours
Effective Hourly Equivalent: $28.85 / hour
Offer B: Higher Hourly Value

Flexible Professional Position

Stated Annual Salary: $55,000.00 / year
Expected Weekly Hours: 35 hours / week
Paid Weeks: 52 weeks (with PTO)
Annual Working Hours: 1,820 hours
Effective Hourly Equivalent: $30.22 / hour

Offer A pays the higher salary ($60,000 vs. $55,000), but Offer B actually pays more per hour of your life ($30.22 vs. $28.85 an hour) because it asks for 260 fewer working hours a year. Those 260 hours are more than six full weeks of your time back — for family, freelancing, study, or rest.

When you compare offers, look at the whole package, not just the salary:

  • Health & Retirement Benefits: Full premium coverage plus a 6% 401(k) match can easily add $8,000 to $12,000 a year in value.
  • Paid Time Off (PTO): Four weeks of PTO instead of two is a real difference in how many hours you actually work.
  • Commute Time & Costs: A remote job saves 5 to 10 hours of unpaid commuting every week, plus thousands of dollars in gas, transit, and car wear. Compare total committed time with our Salary Comparison Calculator.

Common Salary-to-Hourly Calculation Mistakes

Here are six mistakes people make all the time when they convert a salary to an hourly rate:

1

Automatically Assuming Everyone Works 2,080 Hours

2,080 is the standard baseline, but don't just use it blindly if your job asks for 35, 45, or 50 hours a week. Divide by your real hours, or your hourly rate will be wrong.

2

Confusing Paid Time Off With Unpaid Time Off

Don't subtract paid vacation, holidays, or sick leave from your annual hours. Paid time off is already part of your salary. Only unpaid weeks come off.

3

Treating Gross Hourly Pay as Take-Home Pay

Gross hourly pay doesn't account for taxes, Social Security, Medicare, or insurance. Expect your take-home rate to land 20% to 30% below your gross figure.

4

Ignoring Uncompensated Salaried Overtime

If you're an exempt salaried worker regularly putting in 50-hour weeks with no overtime pay, your real hourly rate is 20% lower than the 40-hour figure. Work it out from your actual hours.

5

Overlooking Overtime Eligibility Rules

Plenty of salaried workers assume a salary means no overtime, full stop. If your job duties don't meet the executive or professional exemption rules under the FLSA, you're owed 1.5× overtime pay.

6

Evaluating Base Salary in Complete Isolation

Health insurance, retirement matches, bonuses, and commute costs all count. Total compensation tells you more than base salary on its own.

Limitations

  1. Gross salary only: the conversion starts from gross pay. Taxes, 401(k) contributions, and health premiums change your take-home — not the gross hourly equivalent calculated here.
  2. Hours paid vs. hours worked: dividing by 2,080 gives your rate per paid hour. If you regularly work unpaid extra hours, your rate per hour actually worked is lower.
  3. Salaried overtime rarely pays: most salaried roles are exempt, so hours past 40 add no pay. A conversion cannot capture comp time, bonuses, or on-call expectations built into an offer.
  4. Leave moves the rate both ways: paid vacation raises your rate per hour worked, because the same salary covers fewer worked hours; unpaid leave lowers your effective annual pay below the stated salary.
  5. One salary, one point in time: mid-year raises, signing bonuses, and commission sit outside a base-salary conversion and must be weighed separately. A salary increase calculator shows what a mid-year raise adds across the rest of the year.
  6. A comparison tool, not the whole offer: use the hourly figure to compare offers on equal footing — benefits, schedule control, and job security still decide which offer is really better.

Frequently Asked Questions

Here are straight answers to the questions people ask most about turning a salary into an hourly rate:

How do I calculate my hourly rate from annual salary?

Divide your annual gross salary by the hours you work in a year. If you're full-time at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks, that's 2,080 hours, so you just divide your salary by 2,080. A $60,000 salary works out to about $28.85 an hour before taxes and deductions.

What is $50,000 a year per hour?

$50,000 a year comes to about $24.04 an hour on the standard full-time schedule of 2,080 hours a year (40 hours a week × 52 weeks). That's roughly $961.54 a week gross, or $1,923.08 every two weeks across 26 paychecks. If you work 35 hours a week instead (1,820 hours a year), the same $50,000 is worth $27.47 an hour.

What is $60,000 a year per hour?

On a standard 40-hour week and 52 paid weeks a year (2,080 hours), $60,000 a year is about $28.85 an hour. That works out to $1,153.85 a week, $2,307.69 every two weeks, and $5,000 a month on average, all before payroll deductions. If your job expects 45 hours a week (2,340 hours), your real rate drops to $25.64 an hour.

What is $75,000 a year per hour?

$75,000 a year is about $36.06 an hour on the standard 2,080-hour full-time schedule (40 hours a week for 52 weeks). That's $1,442.31 a week, $2,884.62 every two weeks across 26 pay periods, and $6,250.00 gross a month before federal, state, and local taxes.

What is $100,000 a year per hour?

$100,000 a year is about $48.08 an hour if you work 40 hours a week across 52 weeks (2,080 hours). That's $1,923.08 a week gross, $3,846.15 every two weeks, and $8,333.33 a month before taxes and deductions. Work 50 hours a week instead (2,600 hours), and that same six-figure salary is worth $38.46 an hour.

Does PTO affect my hourly rate?

Paid time off — vacation days, paid holidays, paid sick leave — doesn't cut your gross salary or your standard hourly rate, because you still get your full regular pay while you're away. Unpaid time off is a different story: take 2 unpaid weeks and work 50 weeks instead of 52 (2,000 hours), and your rate while you're actually working rises to $30.00 an hour on a $60,000 salary ($60,000 ÷ 2,000).

Is salary-to-hourly based on gross or net income?

Salary-to-hourly math always works from gross pay, before taxes and deductions. Your take-home hourly rate will be lower once federal income tax, state and local taxes, Social Security (6.2%), Medicare (1.45%), health insurance premiums, and 401(k) contributions come out of each paycheck.

What if I work more than 40 hours a week?

If you're an exempt salaried employee regularly working 45 or 50 hours a week with no extra pay, your real hourly rate falls, because you're splitting the same fixed salary across more hours. If you're non-exempt under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), you're legally owed 1.5 times your regular rate for every hour past 40 in a workweek.

How do I convert a monthly salary to an hourly rate?

To turn a monthly salary into an hourly rate, first multiply it by 12 to get your annual salary, then divide by your annual hours (usually 2,080 for full-time work). Or skip a step and divide your monthly salary by the average hours in a month — about 173.33 hours for a 40-hour week. A $5,000 monthly salary ($60,000 a year) divided by 173.33 hours is $28.85 an hour.

How do I convert a biweekly salary to an hourly rate?

Divide your gross biweekly paycheck by the hours in that pay period — usually 80 hours for a standard full-time two-week schedule. A biweekly paycheck of $2,307.69 divided by 80 hours is about $28.85 an hour.

Key Takeaways

Core Summary Points

  • Divide Salary by Annual Hours: Your gross hourly rate is your annual salary divided by the hours you're scheduled to work in a year.
  • The 2,080 Benchmark: A standard full-time schedule of 40 hours a week across 52 weeks adds up to 2,080 hours a year ($60,000 ÷ 2,080 = $28.85/hr).
  • Work Hours Determine Real Value: On a fixed salary, working 45 or 50 hours a week cuts your real hourly rate.
  • PTO Is Included: Paid time off is part of your salary, so don't subtract paid vacation when you work out your standard hourly rate.
  • Evaluate Total Compensation: When you compare offers, work out the real hourly rate and weigh benefits, commute, and flexibility next to base salary.

How We Calculate Hourly Rates

Our salary-to-hourly calculation divides annual gross salary by total scheduled hours for the year. For full-time work, the benchmark is 40 hours a week over 52 weeks (2,080 hours a year). You can adjust weekly hours, paid weeks, and overtime to match a schedule that's different from the standard. All results are gross earnings, before taxes and withholdings. For the full payroll math and rounding rules, see our Calculation Methodology.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The standard full-time benchmark is 40 hours a week × 52 weeks = 2,080 hours.
  2. Longer weeks lower your effective rate — that same $60,000 salary at 45 hours a week (2,340 hours) is $25.64 an hour.
  3. Paid time off is part of your salary — do not subtract paid vacation when finding your standard hourly rate.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 3, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
